transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 60 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Raj Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Cedarbank CTO), Evan Li (Head of Platform), Priya Kapoor (SRE), Samir Nair (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Agreed next steps to share traffic samples, run benchmark on Dedicated cluster, provide POC proposal and security docs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh I'm Lena from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, quick intros?
[00:00:08] Maya Thompson: Hey I'm Maya, CTO at Cedarbank, we run a customer-facing document summarization chat handler, want to see if Redwood can meet latency and cost needs for production.
[00:00:16] Evan Li: Evan, Head of Platform — I'll own infra for the POC and share traffic samples.
[00:00:19] Raj Patel: Raj, SE at Redwood, I'll handle the benchmark configs and help with workload modelling.
[00:00:23] Priya Kapoor: Priya, SRE, will validate networking and security.
[00:00:27] Samir Nair: Samir, PM working on the pilot scope.

[00:00:35] Lena Ortiz: Cool. Agenda — scoping the POC: success criteria, workload profile (QPS, concurrency), token distribution, and timeline. We have about 45 minutes for technical and then next steps.

[00:00:48] Maya Thompson: To start, our feature is a real-time doc summarizer plus short clarifying chat. Typical session: user uploads doc, we chunk, send prompt to LLM to summarize sections, then followup chat turns. We need sub-second perceived latency for short interactions; long batch jobs are ok to be higher.

[00:01:10] Raj Patel: Nice. Can you share ballpark traffic numbers? average and peak?

[00:01:16] Evan Li: Sure — current average QPS for the endpoint is about 4 QPS, with weekday peaks hitting about 35 QPS over short bursts. Concurrency at peak is typically 18-24 concurrent requests depending on session behavior.

[00:01:28] Raj Patel: That helps. And token lengths? input and expected output?

[00:01:32] Samir Nair: Median input length after chunking ~ 200 tokens, median output ~ 60 tokens. But distribution is heavy-tailed: 70% of calls are sub-300 input tokens, 20% between 300-800, and 10% can be >1000 for large docs. Outputs usually under 150 tokens, but there's a 5% tail that returns 400-800 tokens (longer summaries).

[00:02:00] Lena Ortiz: Great — so we should model both the common short cases and the tail. For POC success criteria, what are your SLOs?

[00:02:07] Maya Thompson: p50 latency for token streaming feels — for the user — we want p50 end-to-end response under 800ms for short prompts, and p99 under 1.2s for the same. For larger summaries we accept higher. Cost target is roughly $0.20 per 1k output tokens equivalent across average workload, we can be flexible if latency is excellent.

[00:02:31] Raj Patel: Okay. Quick clarifying Q: when you say p50/p99, are these per-request end-to-end or per-token generation latency?

[00:02:36] Priya Kapoor: We mean end-to-end from request to first token (perceived interactive latency) and full response completion p95 under 2s for typical short flows.

[00:02:47] Raj Patel: Understood. For modeling, we'll produce both per-token latencies and end-to-end request latencies so you can map to UX.

[00:02:54] Evan Li: Also we need to test both Hosted and Dedicated deployment modes — initial pilot likely Dedicated because of data residency and throughput isolation concerns.

[00:03:02] Lena Ortiz: That makes sense — Dedicated gives predictable throughput. We'll run benchmarks on a Dedicated pool with the model you pick, and we can also show hosted pricing for comparison.

[00:03:11] Raj Patel: On the model side, do you have a preferred family? Smaller quantized models can meet the latency and cost target but may degrade summary quality. Larger models increase token latency. Any evaluation metric constraints?

[00:03:22] Maya Thompson: We need ROUGE-like comparison vs our baseline summarizer, but more importantly a human QA pass on top 200 samples. We'll accept slightly lower automated metrics if human QA is acceptable.

[00:03:33] Raj Patel: Good. For workload characterization, here's the plan I propose: 1) We'll ask for anonymized traffic logs (timestamps, request size in tokens, response size in tokens, user/session id hashed) for 2 weeks. 2) We'll produce a QPS histogram, peak concurrency windows, token distribution CDFs, and a canonical traffic replay script that simulates the same arrival process (Poisson or bursty windows). 3) We'll run progressive benchmarks: low concurrency -> full peak -> long-tail stress tests.

[00:04:03] Evan Li: That sounds right. Could you recommend target concurrency / batch sizes to test? We run on A100-equivalent Dedicated instances.

[00:04:10] Raj Patel: For a start, given your peaks of ~35 QPS and concurrency 18-24, we'll test at 5, 20, and 40 QPS with concurrency up to 48 to test headroom. We'll report p50/p90/p99 and tokens/sec throughput. For batching, we'll test open-loop single request (no batching) and with batching sizes 2-8 to see tradeoffs. We'll also test prefix/KV caching behavior for multi-turn session flows — that often dramatically reduces per-token cost for repeated context.

[00:04:40] Priya Kapoor: On KV cache — we call that KV cash in our notes — but yes. We'll want to see realistic cache hit assumptions. Typical session re-use is about 30% across turns.

[00:04:49] Lena Ortiz: We'll model cache hit rates at 0%, 30%, and 60% to show savings. Also we'll provide quantized model profiles (8-bit/4-bit) with expected latency and throughput curves.

[00:04:59] Maya Thompson: For the POC, we prefer to be conservative on quality, so maybe test both a high-quality full-precision model and a lower-quantized variant to compare quality vs cost.

[00:05:09] Raj Patel: Agreed. We'll provide eval outputs for a subset and run your human QA across them. For latency SLO mapping, note that p99 token emission and end-to-end can diverge if there is long generation. We'll measure both.

[00:05:21] Samir Nair: On timelines — what's realistic? We want to start in two weeks and have a decision within 6 weeks.

[00:05:26] Lena Ortiz: Proposed timeline: share traffic samples this week (Evan), Redwood returns benchmark harness and proposal within 3 business days after that, run benchmarks week of Mar 16, and deliver results + human QA within 2 weeks after the run. Decision meeting by end of March — that fits 6-week window.

[00:05:41] Maya Thompson: That works for us. Regarding security, we'll need SOC2, encryption with KMS, VPC peering, and audit logs. Can you share those docs?

[00:05:49] Lena Ortiz: Yes we'll attach SOC2 cert, security whitepaper, and a checklist for VPC peering and KMS access. For Private deployment we can do customer-managed KMS.

[00:05:58] Priya Kapoor: Also need data retention policy — we want request logs purged after 30 days for POC.

[00:06:02] Raj Patel: Noted. For the benchmark specifics — I'll outline the replay mechanism: we convert your logs into request traces with inter-arrival times preserved for the target window; we also synthesize large-doc flows to exercise >1000 token requests. We'll parameterize the replay to control QPS, concurrency, and cache hit rates.

[00:06:20] Evan Li: On the replay, we can provide a pre-sampled 24h window that includes peak traffic; you can run that to emulate realistic peaks.

[00:06:26] Raj Patel: Perfect. Metrics we will collect: per-request start-to-first-token, token throughput (tokens/sec), p50/p90/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, memory/kv-cache hit ratio, tokens-per-dollar. We'll produce an SLO mapping doc so UX can see expected perceived latency under different arrival profiles.

[00:06:44] Samir Nair: For cost, can you estimate sample numbers? If average QPS 4 and median tokens 260 total per request (in+out), what does that translate to?

[00:06:53] Raj Patel: Rough back-of-envelope: depends on model — for a medium-sized quantized model on Dedicated we might see throughput of ~800-1200 tokens/sec per GPU and cost per 1k tokens maybe $0.10-$0.30 depending on instance amortization and licensing. We'll provide detailed cost model in the proposal with sensitivity to batch size and cache hit rate.

[00:07:10] Maya Thompson: Good enough for planning, but need the exact numbers in the proposal.

[00:07:14] Priya Kapoor: A couple security clarifications: do you support SAML SSO for the console and RBAC for team members?

[00:07:20] Lena Ortiz: Yes SAML SSO and granular RBAC are supported, and we'll include screenshots in the security packet.

[00:07:27] Evan Li: For Dedicated, what's the expected lead time to allocate a small pool for our POC?

[00:07:32] Lena Ortiz: We can reserve Dedicated capacity within a week if there's a commitment to a short trial; otherwise we can run benchmarks on a temporary pool we spin up — provisioning typically 48-72 hours.

[00:07:41] Raj Patel: One more technical note: we'll test both streaming and non-streaming modes. Since you care about perceived latency, streaming first-token times are key — we'll report first-byte times.

[00:07:51] Maya Thompson: Sounds great. Any other blockers from our side?

[00:07:55] Evan Li: None besides us preparing the anonymized logs and confirming network readiness.

[00:07:59] Samir Nair: On evaluation, we'll sample 200 outputs for human QA. We'll need Redwood to highlight differences between model variants.

[00:08:06] Raj Patel: Absolutely. We'll include a diff + side-by-side outputs and a small rubric for human QA scoring.

[00:08:12] Lena Ortiz: Okay let's recap next steps — Evan to send anonymized logs and confirm VPC/KMS readiness; Raj will send benchmark harness and config; Lena will send POC proposal and pricing; Priya will validate network and retention. We'll tentatively schedule the benchmark run week of Mar 16.

[00:08:28] Maya Thompson: Confirmed. Thanks everyone.

[00:08:32] Lena Ortiz: Thanks — I'll follow up with calendar invites and the proposal.

[00:08:36] [end of meeting]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional speaker label mismatch and auto-transcription errors (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache", "Redood" mis-heard).
